comments.name: Mary McNally
comments.body:
My mother was the main caregiver for my dad when he became debilitated by Parkinson’s. My brother and his family lived around the corner from them. He would put Dad to bed every night. My sister-in-law was a godsend. My family is huge but scattered around the country. We all contributed something to the effort. My eldest sister was a registered nurse, so she was the medical advisor. I lived with them for a time, drove them to appointments, and helped them as much as possible around my full-time job. Eventually we hired morning caregivers to assist Dad. Mom had always been a night owl, so that gave her some needed rest. What my brother and I didn’t realize was that she was slipping into dementia. Our siblings noticed it when they visited. 

Ironically Dad’s mind was sharp. He had some hallucinations from the medications he was taking, but he realized he was hallucinating. When it looked like home care was beginning to not be workable and the discussion of assisted living came up, dad asked my mom if she would be going with him. Her response was “no, I’m mobile.” Ironically a couple weeks later she broke her hip and the wheels turned quickly and they were placed together in the same facility. She might have had some event while she had surgery, because afterwards she became frightened and childlike. Being in an unfamiliar environment probably contributed to her fears. They survived only 10 months after the dominoes fell. She passed 40 days after he did.

We waded through 4 inches of slush, (wearing neoprene booties and mitts) and had to push away chunks of ice. We stay in for 5 minutes when it is that cold. But there is a trend quite unusual taking place. It's the "Fondue Immersion."  It takes place in a large tub, the kind you see in cartoons where Mickey is making wine. Made of wood this tub comfortably holds about 10 people. Filled with a  Camembert (the one people rave about) and left out in the sun for about 4 hours, the cheese is soon enough molten. Neighbors and even tourists (from Belgium mostly, though I saw a few Swiss) scamper in and get swallowed up by the yellowish cheese. Frankly, when I did it, I had my doubts. I'm off cheese because of a heart condition but my neighbors Sophie and Jean-Marc insisted it was "le truc à la cannicule."  So we slid into this fromage goo; it stunk and soon people tossed slices of jambon at us. Others aimed baguettes at our heads. Meanwhile the Camembert was so liquid it crept into our every pore, our hair and other areas I can't describe in this family newspaper. I wanted to get out after a minute but Sophie and Jean-Marc insisted I spend a few hours in the tub. "Try to swim," they said. "It's crazy."  

Yes, it was. I didn't get a lot out of it and I still stink of Camembert. Thought it did give me an idea for a comment for the NYT.  I think I might try the Norweigan version next, too. That would be kicking soccer balls in a shark tank with with Erling Haaland.

The Founders created the republic. The Civil War generation preserved the Union and redefined citizenship. The WWII generation built the modern global order. The generation that has governed since roughly 1992 inherited unprecedented military, economic, and technological dominance.

Its legacy is mixed. It oversaw the digital revolution, enormous wealth creation, and remarkable innovation. But it also leaves record debt, political polarization, declining trust in institutions, housing unaffordability, and a foreign policy that often confused military dominance with lasting strategic success.

Rather than seeing this as the end of America, it may be the end of one governing generation’s consensus. History suggests the next generation won’t simply manage decline—it will redefine America’s institutions and priorities for a new era, just as previous generations have done.

Another study (UK Biobank) also confirmed this in healthy populations with no cardiovascular disease in which regular use of fish oil supplements resulting in no primary prevention benefit and instead, an increased risk for atrial fibrillation and also stroke (Chen, 2024). I’ve switched to Turo, which is like Airbnb for cars, and never looked back. Individuals rent out their own vehicles, and many of them are small business owners who maintain a fleet of vehicles. Turo is more affordable than agencies like Enterprise and Hertz, and there are a lot more options, from Nissans to vans to Ferraris. You can filter with the option to pick up from short-term parking at the airport or train station where you’ll be arriving. A lot of time is saved by not having to take an airport shuttle to a traditional rental agency and then inevitably wait in a long line.

Turo vets renters and drivers carefully and has insurance packages for every need. 

I don’t mean to sound like an ad, I just really love Turo! I’ve used it probably a dozen times with no issue.

Some readers wonder why Le Pen is running for the 4th time when she has failed 3 times already. 

French politics work differently than the American version.

In France it is not unheard of to run and fail a couple of times before being elected President. Mitterrand was elected President on the *third* try (1965, 1974, 1981). Chirac as well (1981, 1988, 1995). They both went on to win reelection (Mitterrand in 1988 and Chirac in 2002). 

Legal problems aside, there is nothing strange about Le Pen running again. Especially since her party has gone from a fringe phenomenon to now being the most popular in France. Marine Le Pen herself has seen her score go up with every try: in 2012 she got 18% in the first round and was eliminated; in 2017 she got 21% in the first round and went on to get 34% in the second round; in 2022 she got 23% in the first round and 41.5% in the second round.  

Given this linear progression, her huge popularity, and historical precedent, she has every reason to believe she can clutch victory this time. Which obviously doesn't mean she will, but in her universe it makes sense to try again.

I broke out of it in my early 20s by finally seeing things through with one of my on-again-off-again targets, who contacted me again after some years and he pursued renewing the connection. We had a brief affair and I just let my heart (or pride?) be broken, got mad at him for being evasive, and got over it. What we are seeing in the Pacific is the ripple effect of a retreating U.S. hegemony and increasingly ambiguous commitments to allies that once placed complete trust in the alliance. Middle powers like Australia and Japan, which traditionally relied on U.S. security guarantees, are now losing their strategic orientation in a multipolar world. Fear and uncertainty naturally come first.

Australia, in particular, feels increasingly alone as the only major Anglo-Saxon nation in the region besides NZ. China is stepping into Australia's comfort zone simply because it now can. That doesn't mean China views Australia as a primary threat—far from it. Japan is a bit more concerning for Beijing, although the balance of power still heavily favors China.

China's growing presence in the Pacific is all about military expansion. I think the Chinese leadership has also learned from Japan's failure in World War II. Much of what we see today is deterrence-building aimed primarily at the US in prep for any move against TW. I don't think sending a few Australian or Japanese warships would fundamentally change China's calculations.

Australia needs to learn from its Asian neighbors and decide whether it sees itself primarily as an Asia-Pacific nation or an Anglo-Saxon nation. The same question applies to Japan. Pragmatism has long been the key to how Asian civilization states have coexisted for millennia, and that lesson may become increasingly relevant in the years ahead.

It's a complex engineering system, with precise servos, controllers, sensors, and a control system that dates back to the 90s with software that has been modified by hundreds of people.  All the nuance from lessons learned and institutional knowledge has to be rebuilt.  Some of the exquisite components include a cast silica cap for the radome, a hydraulic system to control the fins, solid fuel pulse motors for terminal attitude control, and a traveling wave tube for the radar.   The missile has been through decades of testing and trials, so re-designing any component involves significant engineering risk and expense.  I hate to say it, but it's not much of a gift to Ukraine.  I would bet that one of the defense startups like Andruil would have better luck designing a replacement that would be cheaper and much easier to manufacture with modern electronics, CPUs and software.

Given that ballistic missile interception at scale is a strategic necessity, replacing Patriot with a economic alternative is a priority for the US and its allies.

I would like to see a reasonably faithful adaptation of the whole series.  I got to know the Ingalls family from the books, which my mother read to me before I knew there was a television series—and I only ever managed to watch a few episodes of that, finding them utterly unlike the stories in the books.  But I think we stopped after *By the Shores of Silver Lake*.  I think Mary's illness was too much for me to handle, and perhaps my mother sensed I wouldn't be as interested in Laura growing up in the later books, though seeing them on the shelf always intrigued me.

I disagree with the use of "novels" and "fiction" to describe the books.  Yes, the episodes were edited and no doubt the stories retold to bring together things that really happened at different times, the events simplified and told out of order—much as they might be in real-life reminiscences—but still basically truth.  Perhaps "fictionalized" would be a fairer description.

The original works contain truths that are uncomfortable today.  The pioneers weren't enlightened; they were afraid of the Indians and had reason to be, just as the Indians had reason to resent white settlers.  When Pa participated in a minstrel show, he didn't think he was doing anything to harm or demean black folks.  We cringe when we read these things today, but they were the realities with which the people of another age lived.  And they could be presented fairly, with context, by a sensitive adaptation.  That would be worth seeing.

Greater ethnic diversity in television and film is, on balance, is a positive development. But when historical dramas begin rewriting the past in the name of present-day values, they risk replacing one false narrative with another.
What happens when future generations grow up watching new period dramas like Little House on the Prairie and Bridgerton and come away believing that 18th and 19th-century society was broadly inclusive? How are they supposed to grasp the depth of slavery, segregation, exclusion, and the everyday humiliations that minorities endured if those realities are softened, minimized, or simply written out of the story?
History isn't valuable because it's comforting. It's valuable because it's true. Sanitizing the past -- whether to make it more inclusive, more patriotic, or more politically convenient -- doesn't promote justice; it promotes historical amnesia.
The impulse to rewrite history isn't confined to one ideology. Whether it's Hollywood reshaping the past to reflect contemporary cultural values or politicians pressuring museums and public institutions to tell a more flattering national story, the result is the same: future generations inherit mythology instead of history. And a society that forgets what really happened is far more likely to repeat it.

comments.body: A significant problem with sea temps around Britain is the shallowness of the waters. For some years now signs of human habitation have been dredged up from the North Sea off East Anglia. The 'land bridge' between Britain and what is now the coast of Europe, was dry land, now known a 'Doggerland' after the Dogger Bank,. Its average depth is around 15 to 20 meters (about 50–65 feet), with some parts as shallow as 13 meters. Sustained high temps will heat up this water considerably added to which the North Sea is somewhat akin to a marine lake. The waters that drain out of it down the English Channel run back 6 hours later.

comments.name: Metaphor

So if I may quibble a bit, are the oceans getting hotter or are they getting warmer? I mean, for something to be getting hotter it sort of has to be hot to begin with. It's like saying that when water boiling at 100 Celsius lowers its temperature to 99 Celsius it is getting "colder." I guarantee that if you stick your hand in 99 Celsius water you are going to get a nasty burn from water that is "colder" than 100 Celsius, in which case it hardly seems appropriate to compare 99 to 100 and say that the former is "colder" than the latter.

I suppose my point is that human-caused climate change is undeniable, but when the news media are careless with their use of language it only gives support to climate deniers who see nothing but hysteria in the media's reporting on climate change.

Thanks for reporting on this subject. It's sad to see the terrible effect on sea life from these ocean heat waves. And this ocean heat has other grave implications.

There are parts of the system that are already out of our hands. And those parts are related to the ocean. Because we know that we’ve already put a lot of heat content into the ocean. 

And in the case of the Antarctic Ice Sheet, regarding the marine based ice which is very sensitive to ocean temperatures—West Antarctica 3.3 meters of sea level rise equivalent of ice, East Antarctica 19 meters—we are committed to some response of the ice sheet to the heat that has already gone into the ocean. And Greenland has around 3 meters worth of marine based ice as well.

How much response? According to the paleoclimate record at 1.5-2°C above preindustrial temperature around 6-9 meters of sea level rise (we’re likely already committed to at least 2°C)
At 3°C, tens of meters eventually.

Times scales are the big question and the community in general has been conservative with time scales.

The real pioneer of introspective filmmaking was Ed Pincus, who was McElwee's teacher at MIT. But Ross did not merely ape Pincus's confessional diary films. There's a level of irony in Sherman's March, hints that the first person address to the camera is as much performed as genuine, that McElwee is an unreliable narrator, and the idea he truly originally intended to make a film about Sherman is nonsense. (Fun trivia fact for documentary nerds: the narration at the beginning is voiced by Ricky Leacock.) Anyway, what McElwee certainly accomplished was adapting the diary form to films that had much broader appeal, played in theaters, got shown on PBS, had DVD releases. There's a reason Ed Pincus's work is not well known. It's too close to the bone.
Another documentary filmmaker who no doubt inspired McElwee to some extent is Michael Rubbo, who created the form of a film that unfolds out of the failure to complete some other ostensible project. Rubbo's Waiting for Fidel is most directly the template for Roger and Me, and Nick Broomfield's solo films, but along with Sherman's March they show that era had a current of filmmaker-as-character imbued with cheek.

The carbon cycle for the last 2 million years was doing 180-280ppm atmospheric CO2 over 10,000 years and we’ve done more change than that in 100 years. The speed of change now is much greater than virtually anything we have found in Earth’s climate history.

The last time CO2 went from 180-280ppm global temperature increased by around 4 degrees C and sea level rose 130 meters. (See graph below, 1) It takes time for temperature and sea level to equilibrate with elevated atmospheric CO2 and we could blow much further off of that graph.

One amplifying feedback alone out of dozens, loss of albedo or heat reflectivity from Arctic summer sea ice melt, over the last several decades has been equivalent to 25 percent of the climate forcing of anthropogenic CO2. And that will continue to increase as that ice largely disappears by mid century.

The Titanic sank because by the time the lookout called the warning the ship had too much momentum to turn. The Earth has a lot more momentum, e.g. we've already likely locked in at least 6 meters of sea level rise from the Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets and decade to decade warming in the near term is also virtually locked in.

That momentum is building and the higher we let global temperatures rise the greater the risk of them going really high as amplifying feedbacks strengthen.

1.  (graph of the last 400,000 years of global temperature, CO2 and sea level https://www.ces.fau.edu/nasa/images/impacts/slr-co2-temp-400000yrs.jpg )

The ocean for many is out of sight and mind. But Atlantic fish stocks 10 years ago were between 1/1,000 and 1/10,000 of what they were just 150 to 200 years ago. (1) 

The continental shelves used to be forests of sponges and corals, critical habitat for fish development.

Trawling has reduced to mud, to parking lot, a greater area of the ocean floor than the area of forests cut down in the history of humanity.

Over hunting and fishing, habitat loss, invasive species, pollution and now climate change.

None of these things happen in a vacuum, but there are synergies among them which make the whole vastly greater than the sum of the parts.

We are a water planet and as goes the ocean go we.

Bus riders need more bus capacity, more frequent buses and more bus routes – bus lanes are not “the solution” if there are no buses.

Getting rid of bus stops actually makes a longer “trip” overall - because riders need to walk further to get the bus.
